items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Hassett et al.’s (2008) study of monkey toy preferences. Include at least one point about ecological validity.
items.answer: Strength (controls): Each test paired one wheeled and one plush toy, and different toys were used across sessions, so the preference was for the category of toy rather than one particular object. Strength (ecological validity): The monkeys lived in a large social troop in an outdoor enclosure and were observed with their normal social group, so their behaviour was relatively natural. Weakness (reliability of observations): Decisions about what counted as an interaction were made by observers watching video; if only one observer coded each behaviour, inter-rater reliability may be limited. Weakness (nature versus nurture): Even monkeys experience some social learning in a troop (for example from mothers), so the study cannot completely rule out the influence of socialisation. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. items.stem: Evaluate Hassett et al.’s (2008) study of monkey toy preferences, including a discussion of quantitative data.
items.answer: Strength (quantitative data): Frequency and duration of interactions with each toy were recorded from video, so preferences of males and females could be compared objectively. Strength (ethics): The monkeys were not harmed or deprived; they were simply offered toys in their normal enclosure, which may even have been enriching. Weakness (generalisability): The findings come from rhesus monkeys, whose brains and social lives differ from humans’, so it cannot be assumed that the same explanation applies to children. Weakness (nature versus nurture): Even monkeys experience some social learning in a troop (for example from mothers), so the study cannot completely rule out the influence of socialisation. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: ‘The use of animals in Hassett et al.’s study can be justified.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: Arguments for: Monkeys allowed toy preference to be studied without human gender socialisation, which would be impossible with children. The monkeys were not harmed and lived in their normal social group. Arguments against: Animals cannot consent, and keeping primates in captivity raises ethical questions. The findings may not generalise to humans, so the benefit is uncertain. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: In a replication of Hassett et al. at a primate centre near Lisbon, the time (seconds) that each of 9 male monkeys spent interacting with a wheeled toy and a plush toy in one 25-minute session was recorded. Table: Time spent interacting (seconds) — Wheeled toy: 66, 46, 65, 57, 45, 45, 120, 70, 57. Plush toy: 41, 28, 42, 34, 37, 56, 18, 45, 30. (a) Explain why the median may be a better measure of central tendency than the mean for the wheeled toy condition. (b) The participants were shoppers who happened to pass Felix in a shopping centre in Lisbon. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it. (c) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results. (d) Explain why a independent measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) The score of 120 is an extreme score (outlier) compared with the rest of the wheeled toy data; the mean is distorted by it, but the median is not affected by extreme values, so it is more representative. (b) Opportunity sampling. Weakness: only people at that shopping centre at that time could be chosen, so the sample may be biased and results may not generalise. (c) Counterbalance the order, so half do condition A first and half do condition B first, to reduce the effect of order effects. (d) Independent measures avoids order effects and makes it harder to guess the aim, but participant variables between the two groups could then explain the results, and more participants are needed.

items.stem: ‘Sex differences in toy preference are mainly caused by biological factors.’ Discuss this view. In your answer, you may refer to nature versus nurture and animal research.
items.answer: Arguments for: Male rhesus monkeys, who are not exposed to human gender stereotypes, preferred wheeled toys, as boys do (Hassett et al.). Prenatal androgens are linked to masculine play (for example girls with congenital adrenal hyperplasia). Arguments against: Female monkeys showed no strong preference, unlike human girls, suggesting that human preferences are partly learned. Children are rewarded and shown toys by parents and media (socialisation). Monkeys may not generalise to humans. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.answer: (a) They are numerical counts (tallies) of how often each behavioural category occurred, so they can be totalled and compared. items.stem: Evaluate Hassett et al.’s (2008) study of monkey toy preferences in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about generalisability.
items.answer: Strength (quantitative data): Frequency and duration of interactions with each toy were recorded from video, so preferences of males and females could be compared objectively. Strength (ecological validity): The monkeys lived in a large social troop in an outdoor enclosure and were observed with their normal social group, so their behaviour was relatively natural. Weakness (reliability of observations): Decisions about what counted as an interaction were made by observers watching video; if only one observer coded each behaviour, inter-rater reliability may be limited. Weakness (generalisability): The findings come from rhesus monkeys, whose brains and social lives differ from humans’, so it cannot be assumed that the same explanation applies to children. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how hormones might influence children’s toy preferences. (b) Explain why studying monkeys can help to resolve the nature–nurture debate about toy preference.
items.answer: (a) Exposure to androgens such as testosterone before birth may organise the developing brain in a more male-typical way, leading to interest in toys involving movement, such as vehicles. (b) Monkeys do not experience human gender stereotypes about toys, so if they still show sex differences, these are more likely to be due to biological factors.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe the results of Hassett et al.’s study. (b) Explain the conclusion Hassett et al. drew from their results.
items.answer: (a) Male monkeys consistently preferred wheeled toys, interacting with them more often and for longer; females interacted with both types and did not show a significant preference; the pattern was similar to human children’s toy preferences. items.stem: Plan a questionnaire to investigate whether parents encourage boys and girls to play with different toys. Your plan must include: the types of questions, how the data will be analysed, the sampling technique and one example question.
items.answer: Method: a questionnaire. Closed questions (for example rating scales from 1 to 5) for quantitative data and at least one open question for qualitative detail; pilot the questions; avoid leading questions. Variables: topic: parental encouragement; measure: rating scales and open answers. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Karachi, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.answer: Arguments for: Monkeys allowed toy preference to be studied without human gender socialisation, which would be impossible with children.
